evidence: Cic. Lael. 95: cīvis sevērus et gravis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Grave and strict in look and conduct; of judges, stern; of people who live soberly, austere (Catull. 27.6). Severity is sevēritās (Tac. Agr. 9.4). Only rarely in a bad sense, harsh (Lewis & Short). It also means serious, not joking (see serious).

evidence: Ter. Heaut. 439: satis jam satis pater dūrus fuī
Ter. Ph. 497: adeōne ingeniō esse dūrō tē atque inexōrābilī …?
terms.comment: Its first sense is hard to the touch (see hard). Of a person, hard and unbending, where sevērus is strict but just; a father is dūrus in Terence when he has been too harsh.

terms.gloss: stern, strict; of taste, harsh, dry
evidence: Cic. Cael. 33: illō austērō mōre ac modō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: From Greek αὐστηρός: of wine and fruit, harsh and dry to the taste (Cato, Celsus); of a person or a style, stern and unsmiling. Not before Cicero in this sense (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: harsh, bitter; strict (of someone in authority)

phrases.english: But here he comes out himself: how stern he looks!

phrases.latin: Nōn possum: satis jam satis pater dūrus fuī.
phrases.english: I can’t: I have been a harsh father long enough, more than enough.

phrases.latin: vīvāmus, mea Lesbia, atque amēmus, rūmōrēsque senum sevēriōrum omnēs ūnius aestimēmus assis!
phrases.english: let us live, my Lesbia, and love, and value all the mutterings of stern old men at a single penny!

phrases.latin: ipse nec habeat vitia nec ferat. nōn austēritās ejus trīstis, nōn dissolūta sit cōmitās
phrases.english: let the teacher have no faults and put up with none; let his strictness not be gloomy, nor his friendliness slack
